lines.text: A Bird, came down the Walk -
He did not know I saw -
He bit an Angle Worm in halves
And then, he drank a Dew
And then hopped sidewise to the Wall
They looked like frightened Beads, I thought,
Or Butterflies, off Banks of Noon,

notes.body: The bird acts like an roving criminal, moving without being witnessed and attacking the worm without a shred of compunction.

The internal near-rhyme of 'fellow' and 'raw' evokes the strange, almost foreign, brutality of the bird.
To the poet both worm and bird alike are fellow creatures to be encountered in nature,
but the bird's act of necessity cruelly undercuts any kind of convivial pretensions that the poet may project upon them.

Despite the seemingly brutal act committed by the bird in the first stanza,
the poet continues to see the bird in the light of human custom.
Here, the bird drinks a dew from a 'convenient' Grass.
The bird so courteously leaves space for another member of the insect-folk to pass - how amiable!

The poet uses the movement of the eyes to keenly evoke the sense of unease.
Dickinson's adoption of 'Beads,' inanimate round objects,
almost makes the bird's eyes fall out of their sockets from fear.

The portrayal of the bird as a cautious, paranoid agent culminates with the first sign of the poet's intervention
within the happenings of nature. The poet offers the bird 'a Crumb.' What is the reason for this?
Has the poet felt the bird's fright within herself?
Is the crumb really for the bird's benefit or is the offering a soothing measure for the human being's sense of inner fright?

The bird unrolls his feathers into flight. Has the bird taken the crumb with him? Or has he ultimately been frightened into escape?
For the poet that gazes upon the flying bird, she keeps her association, still, of the movements of the bird
with that of human action - rowing.

The poet imagines the bird's flight through the traces left by oars moving in water, so light and ephemeral they barely form a seam
upon the water's silver surface. In a beautiful moment of inversion, as if the eyes of the reader are meant to see the
sky above reflected on the watery mirror-surface, the bird has metaphorically transformed into a lightsome butterfly.
It leaps, plashlessly, as it swims.

In these moments of the poem, the poet anthropomorphises the bird and other creatures around her.
The bird is not simply a bird to be observed, but the medium through which the poet can vicariously live
out both the cruelties and sublimities of nature.

The poet's empathetic projection into the bird's life tilts from one extreme state to
to another: from a vision of unfettered crime, to listless paranoia, ultimately to a kind of domestic return.
By throwing herself into the bird's life, the poet reclaims for herself a vast spectrum of
of feelings that could not have been disclosed within the limited bounds of domestic husbandry,
of mere feeding of an animal, the offering of 'a Crumb.'

This almost exultant last stanza is suspiciously devoid of the roving bird.
It makes you wonder whether the poem was ever about the bird at all, in truth,
or whether the bird's deft movements simply brought off the poet's movement
into artistic freedom, culminating in a series of dense metaphors whereby
the wings are oars, the air is water, and time substantialises into place - a "Bank of Noon".
